input.question: [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
My name is Participant, and I work long days in the small office near the taxi rank, always hustling to keep the files straight and handle clients who sometimes come before the sun is up. Every morning, I grab a quick brown bread sandwich—sometimes just tea if I’m running late, no sugar because I know my sugar must stay low, hey. But you know what? I have never really thought about how skipping breakfast or sitting all day might make me feel tired and sore. Yesterday, my boss asked me to pack a pile of boxes away, but halfway, I just felt so heavy! I tried to lift, but I ended up sitting down, breathless. I always thought, 'Isn’t working at the office enough exercise already?'

Later that afternoon I went to the local clinic to collect my medication. [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] Sihle—she’s always so patient—looked at me and asked why I was sweating. I told her about the boxes. She smiled and shook her head, telling me softly, 'Participant, you don’t need a gym. Try using a chair for squats, water bottles for light weight, even sweeping the yard. Little things, every day, neh? It adds up.' I frowned because, honestly, where do I even start when home already feels full of work? But [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] Sihle explained, 'Even five minutes stretches before your tea, or dancing with your child in the kitchen. Make it fun.' She made it sound so easy—could it really work?

The next morning was harder than I thought. I set my phone alarm, telling myself, 'Today, Participant, just five minutes.' But I felt funny, doing squats on the lounge chair while my daughter watched cartoons. I nearly gave up when the spoon fell from my hand during arm lifts—can you imagine? I giggled, but I wanted to stop. Then I remembered, next week I must help set up tables for our community talk at work. That’s a bigger job. If I don’t try now, will I be strong enough for that?

Each day, I added one more minute, sometimes resting, sometimes sweating and laughing. By the time the work event came, I was ready. I lifted chairs, walked back and forth, and didn’t feel short of breath or embarrassed. My coworkers smiled, surprised. Now, I don’t wait to be tired to get moving. Sure, a gym is good for some people, but this is my gym: my home, my family, and every small movement I do. Who knew simple things could change so much?

input.question: [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
I’m Participant, a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] working in a busy clinic in the [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]. Every day I rush to work, and I often eat late at night — after shifts, when my body is tired. I know I have diabetes and high blood pressure, but I don’t really understand how eating late affects my blood sugar. My parents say I should eat better, but I just think, ‘I’ll eat tomorrow.’ I used to eat umxhentso with my friends after work, but now I eat chips and sweets because they’re easy. I don’t feel sick, so I don’t think it matters. That’s how I keep going — just because I don’t feel bad doesn’t mean it’s not hurting my body.

One night, after a long shift, I went to the local clinic for my check-up. The [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], Nandi, asked me about my diet. I said I eat late, and she looked at me and said, ‘Participant, when you eat late, your blood sugar goes up — it’s like a rollercoaster. You can’t just eat chips and sweets and expect it to be fine.’ I said, ‘But I don’t feel anything.’ She smiled and said, ‘That’s the problem — your body doesn’t tell you, but your blood does.’ She gave me a simple plan: eat a small portion of vegetables and grilled chicken, like in a stir-fry, and drink water. She said, ‘Start with one meal a week — just one. It’s not a big change, but it will help your body feel better.’ I was surprised, but I said yes. I didn’t know how to start, but I felt like I had a chance.

I tried the stir-fry on my first night — chicken, spinach, and carrots — but I forgot to eat it before bed. I ate it with my friend Participant after work, and we had chips and lemonade instead. I felt guilty, but I didn’t stop. I thought, ‘Maybe I just need to be patient.’ The next week, I tried again — this time I made it with my sister. She said, ‘Participant, you’re doing it right — just one meal a week is enough to start.’ But I still didn’t feel strong. I missed the umxhentso dance with my friends. I was sad. But then I remembered: next month, I have to lead a health workshop for young nurses at the clinic. I can’t go in with a tired body or high blood sugar. That’s when I decided to keep going — even if it’s hard.

After a few weeks, I started eating the stir-fry every Friday night. I added a little lemon and herbs, and I drank water before bed. My blood sugar stayed steady, and I felt more awake. I even taught my sister how to make it. At the health workshop, I showed the recipe and said, ‘This is how I changed my life — one small step at a time.’ The nurses smiled and said, ‘Participant, you’re doing great.’ I didn’t just feel better — I felt proud. I now know that my body is not just a machine. It listens. And when I listen, I can dance, work, and live well. I still dance umxhentso — but now I do it after I eat the right food. That’s how I found peace.

input.question: [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
I wake up early, like every day, and go to work at the local clinic. I'm an [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], so I have to manage papers and help the nurses. My job is important, and I don’t want to miss a day. But I don’t really think about how my body feels. I eat what’s on the table — samp and beans, sometimes with a bit of salt and oil. I don’t know much about blood sugar or blood pressure. I just eat because it’s what we do. My husband says I should be more careful, but I don’t listen. I think my body is strong. I don’t believe I need to change anything. I just want to finish my work and go home.

One day, the clinic [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] says, 'Participant, you’ve been coming for years, but your blood pressure is going up. Your doctor says you need to eat less salt and more greens. You can cook with pumpkin leaves or spinach — they’re cheap and good for your heart.' I say, 'But I don’t have time. I have work to do. And my family eats the same food.' She says, 'You don’t need to change everything. Just one thing — make a green stew one day a week. It’s simple, and it helps your blood.' I nod, but I don’t believe it will work. I just want to keep doing what I know. I don’t trust that a new food will make me feel better.

I try to make the green stew. I go to the market and buy pumpkin leaves. I chop them and cook with a little oil. It tastes bitter at first. I don’t like it. I eat it with my porridge, but I feel tired. The next day, I forget. I go back to eating beans and samp with salt. My son says I look tired. I tell him I’m fine. I think the work is more important than food. But then I hear that the clinic is starting a group for older women — a cooking class — and it’s on the next week. I feel a little scared. I don’t want to fail again. But I know if I don’t go, I’ll miss the chance to learn how to cook healthy food for my family.

I go to the cooking class. The woman teaches us how to cook with greens, beans, and maize. I try again — this time with spinach and a little onion. It’s not perfect, but I like it. I cook it for my husband and son. They say it tastes better than before. I feel strong. I don’t feel tired anymore. I start making it every week. I even share the recipe with my neighbour. I don’t think I’ll ever stop. Because now I know — my body is not just a machine. It’s part of my work, my family, my life. And I can take care of it, even when I’m busy.

Every morning, I wake up like a clock, and I go straight to the kitchen. I think, 'What’s for breakfast?' My wife says, 'Participant, the bread is still warm, and there’s a pot of milk.' I grab a slice of white bread and pour milk on it. I don’t even think about blood sugar. I just eat. 'Why would bread make me feel tired?' I ask myself. 'I’m a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], I need energy to teach.' But after a while, I feel weak, my hands shake, and I have to sit down. I don’t know why. I thought I was strong. Then I remember, I used to eat at the school canteen — they had rice and beans. That felt good. But today, I didn’t feel good. I just wanted to go to work and teach. I didn’t think about what I was eating. That’s when I started to wonder — is it the food or just me? Maybe I need to change what I eat.

One day, I went to the clinic. The [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], a young woman named Nomsa, looked at me and said, 'Participant, you have diabetes. Your body needs to know what to eat.' I said, 'But I eat what’s easy. I don’t want to change.' She smiled and said, 'Not everything is hard. We can start small. Try eating more beans, lentils, and green vegetables. No sugar, no white bread. These foods don’t make your blood sugar go up fast.' I said, 'But I don’t like beans. They taste bitter.' She said, 'Try them with a little salt and a bit of onion. It will taste better. And you can cook them with your old pot — the one you use for stew.' I said, 'Okay, I’ll try.' I didn’t believe it would help, but I wanted to go to the next meeting — a community health day — and I needed to feel strong.

I tried beans the next day. I cooked them with onion and a little salt. I ate them with a piece of brown bread. But my wife said, 'Participant, you didn’t eat the green beans — you only ate the beans.' I said, 'I didn’t know they were green beans.' I thought beans were just the same. The next day, I felt a little better. But I still drank milk and ate white bread in the evening. My feet started to feel hot. I felt tired. I thought, 'I must be doing something wrong.' Then I remembered — I have to go to the community health day next week. I need to be strong to speak about health. So I said to myself, 'I can’t fail this time. I’ll eat only what helps me stay clear and strong.' I started to plan meals. I made a list: beans, spinach, carrots, and lentils. I even cooked them with my old pot — just like Nomsa said.

After a week, I started to feel different. I didn’t feel weak in the afternoon. I could walk to the church without resting. My wife said, 'Participant, you look better. You’re not shaking anymore.' I said, 'Yes, I am. I eat what helps my body. I don’t eat white bread or sugar. I eat beans, green vegetables, and brown bread. I even made a stew with carrots and lentils — it tasted good. I told the community group at the health day, 'I used to think food didn’t matter. Now I know it does.' They all smiled. I felt proud. I didn’t just change my food — I changed how I think. I now know that small changes, like eating beans, can make a big difference. I will keep going. I will teach others how to eat well, too.

input.story:
I used to eat bread with butter every morning before I went to work, and I thought, 'What’s wrong with that?' My blood sugar would go up fast, and I’d feel tired by midday. I didn’t know that bread, even white bread, could make my body work harder. I just thought, 'I’m fine, I’ve been doing it for years.' But then I saw my boss, Thandi, she had a headache and couldn’t focus. She said, 'Participant, I need you to help me with the community clean-up this weekend. We’re going to clean the old schoolyard near the bus stop.' I said yes, but I didn’t know it would mean I had to change what I eat. I didn’t think health would matter in work. How could it? I was just a worker, not a doctor.

One day, at the clinic, a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] named Nomsa told me, 'Participant, you don’t need to eat bread with butter every day. Try eating brown rice or chapati instead. They don’t spike your sugar like white bread does. And you can add a little onion or green pepper, not sugar. Your body will feel better, and you’ll have more energy to work.' I said, 'But I’m used to bread, Nomsa. What if I feel weak?' She smiled and said, 'Try one meal with chapati this week. Just one. You’ll see how you feel.' I didn’t believe it at first, but I thought, 'What if it helps me do the clean-up better? Maybe I can help more than just clean.'

I tried chapati on Tuesday, but I forgot to eat it. I went to work and had bread with butter again. By afternoon, I felt dizzy and my hands shook. I sat down at my desk and said, 'Participant, what did I do wrong?' I thought, 'I can’t keep doing this. I need to eat better.' The next day, I told Nomsa about it. She said, 'Just eat chapati with a little curry and a glass of water. No sugar. And try it every day for three days.' I did it. But on Thursday, I was too tired and ate a piece of cake because I was stressed. I felt worse. I thought, 'Maybe I can’t do it.' But then I remembered the clean-up. If I don’t feel strong, I won’t help the community. I had to try again.

After five days, I started eating chapati every morning. I added a little green pepper and a small piece of boiled egg. I felt stronger, clearer, and I could walk to the bus stop without feeling weak. When the clean-up day came, I helped carry tools, and I even taught the kids how to sort waste. I saw Thandi smiling and said, 'Participant, you’re doing great!' I said, 'I didn’t think I could, but I did it. Maybe I can do more. Maybe I can help others eat better too.' I now know that food isn’t just about taste — it’s about how my body feels. And when I feel strong, I can do more for my family and my community.

input.story:
Every morning, I wake up like any other [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] — the sun is rising, the school bell is ringing, and I’m already hungry. I grab a loaf of bread from the shop, and it’s white and soft, like the kind my mum used to buy. I eat it with a little butter and a banana. I think, 'Is this good for my body?' But I don’t know. I just know I feel tired after class, and my hands shake a bit. I play football with the boys after school, and we eat chips and soda. I don’t think about sugar or blood sugar — I just eat because I’m hungry. My small work task? To make a poster for the school health fair. I started with a drawing of a banana and a plate, but I didn’t know what to put next. My [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] said, 'Participant, you need to show how food helps your body.' I didn’t know how. I just drew a big red circle and wrote 'Eat more!' — and that was it. It didn’t feel right.

Then one day, I went to the clinic. I sat with Mrs. Nkosi, a kind lady with glasses and a calm voice. She asked me, 'Participant, what do you eat every day?' I told her about the bread, the banana, the chips. She smiled and said, 'You’re doing good, but some foods can make your blood sugar go up fast. For a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] like you, try eating brown rice, lentils, beans, and fresh vegetables — like spinach, carrots, and cabbage. These don’t spike your sugar. And no sugar in drinks!' I said, 'But what about my football game? I need energy!' She said, 'You can have a little energy from a banana, but not too much. And eat it with a spoonful of chia or flaxseed — that’s better.' I didn’t believe it at first. I thought, 'Can I really eat beans and not feel tired?' But she gave me a list with pictures — a plate with brown rice, a green leaf, a red bean. I felt like I was learning something real. I said, 'I’ll try it.' I didn’t know if I could, but I had to try for the poster.

The next week, I tried the lentils and spinach. I cooked them with a little oil and ate them with a slice of wholemeal bread. I felt full, not tired. I didn’t feel shaky after class. I even had a little energy to help my students with their homework. But one day, I forgot to eat the lentils and ate chips again. I felt dizzy and my hands shook. I thought, 'Oh no, I failed.' But I remembered the poster — I had to show the school how to eat well. So I didn’t give up. I made a new poster: 'Eat Brown Rice, Beans, and Greens — They Keep Your Energy Strong!' I added a picture of a football player eating a bowl of beans with a smile. I showed it to my [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], and she said, 'Participant, you’re doing it right.' I felt proud. I knew I could do more — not just for the poster, but for my body and my future work.

Now, I eat beans every day. I even teach my students about it. I show them how to cook lentils with spices, how to eat spinach with a little oil. I play football, and I eat a banana with chia seeds after. My blood sugar doesn’t spike. I feel strong. I don’t feel tired. I even got a chance to lead a health workshop at school — for the whole grade. I told them, 'Participant once didn’t know what food was good for his body. Now he knows. And so can you.' The kids clapped. I felt happy. I didn’t just change my food — I changed my life. And I know, if I keep going, I can help more people.

input.question: [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
My name is Participant, and I teach history at a school in East London. It’s a tough job, lots of kids, lots of paperwork – I’m always running around. Most days, I grab a quick pap and beans for breakfast, maybe a loaf of bread with a bit of cheese if I’m feeling fancy. Lunch is usually something from a spaza shop – maybe a wors or a samoosa. Dinner… well, dinner is often whatever’s easiest, sometimes just a packet of maize meal with a little gravy. I don't really think about my blood sugar much, you know? Just get through the day. Yesterday, I had to prepare a presentation on the Battle of Isandlwana for the grade 10s, and I was so busy rushing around getting everything ready that I forgot to eat properly. I felt lightheaded halfway through, and the whole thing just kind of… fizzled out. The kids were disappointed, and honestly, I was too. It wasn’t my best work.

Today, I went to the clinic for my check-up. [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] Zola was really kind. She looked at my blood pressure and then at my sugar levels – they were a bit high, she said. She explained that when I skip meals or eat sugary things, my body struggles to handle the sugar properly, especially with the insulin I take. She said it’s like my body is saying, ‘Hey, slow down! I need a break!’ She showed me a simple chart with what to eat – lots of vegetables, whole grains, and less meat. She told me to try and have a small snack, like some fruit or nuts, before the afternoon classes. It sounded complicated, but she made it seem really manageable. She also told me to check my sugar levels more often, just to see how I’m doing. It felt a bit strange, but also… helpful. It’s good to know there’s someone paying attention, and that it’s not just me struggling alone.

I tried to follow her advice, honestly I did. I made sure to have a small bowl of porridge with some fruit for breakfast, and I packed a handful of peanuts for a snack during my break. But it was hard, you know? I’m used to grabbing a quick biscuit or a sugary drink when I’m feeling peckish. And then, after school, I was exhausted, and the thought of cooking a proper meal felt overwhelming. I ended up having a packet of biscuits with a cup of tea – and my sugar shot right up! I felt a bit shaky afterwards, and it made me realize just how much of a habit it is. It wasn’t a big deal, just a little slip-up, but it made me feel a bit discouraged. I almost gave up, thinking, ‘What’s the point?’

But then I remembered Mr. Participant, the school principal, told me about the school sports day next month. He needs volunteers to help with the activities, and I really want to be involved. I want to show my kids that even though I’m a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], I can still be active and healthy. So, I’ve started small – I’m walking to school instead of taking the bus whenever I can, and I’m trying to eat a bit healthier each day. My sugar levels are still a bit wonky sometimes, but they’re getting better. I feel more energetic, and I’m actually starting to enjoy the process of taking care of myself. It’s not about being perfect, it’s about making small changes that add up over time. And honestly, that feels like a real victory.

input.story:
The sun’s already beating down, even this early, and I’m already chasing after crates of mangoes for the market. It’s a good day for business, a busy one. I usually just grab a quick cup of maize porridge – nothing fancy, you know? – and a few peanuts before heading out. It’s all I can manage before the day really kicks off. Honestly, I don't think too much about what I’m eating, just need something to keep me going. Today, I rushed out, grabbed a handful of peanuts, and headed straight to the stall. But halfway through the morning, my stomach started feeling funny, and I just couldn’t seem to finish the day’s work. I felt weak and dizzy, and had to sit down for a while. It was frustrating, a real waste of time and money.

Later, Dr. Zola called me in at the clinic. She listened patiently as I explained how I felt, and then she looked at my blood sugar readings. She said, ‘Participant, you’re not getting enough fiber in your diet, and those quick snacks aren’t helping your blood sugar stay stable.’ She explained that a balanced diet, with regular meals and snacks, is really important for keeping your energy levels up and preventing those dizzy spells. She suggested I start with a small bowl of cooked beans or a piece of fruit with a handful of nuts, and to drink plenty of water throughout the day. input.story:
My name is Participant, and I teach at the school in Buffalo City. It’s a good school, lots of kids, but sometimes, it feels like I’m running around like a headless chicken! I usually have a sadza and beans for breakfast – it’s quick, you know? And then maybe some veggies if I have time. Lunch is usually something from the tuck shop – a bunny chow, or maybe a boerewors roll. It’s yummy, but sometimes my tummy feels a bit funny afterwards. I don't really think much about it, though. I just get on with the day, teaching my little ones about history and reading. It’s important work, but honestly, sometimes I forget to take care of myself. I think, ‘Later, Participant, later.’

Today, I had to prepare a presentation about the history of the Xhosa people for the school’s heritage day. I promised Mr. Dube, the principal, I’d have it ready by lunchtime. I planned to make some pap with beetroot for my lunch, thinking that would give me energy for the afternoon. But I got so busy with the kids, helping them with their writing and explaining the stories, I completely forgot to check my blood sugar. By the time I realised, it was almost 3 pm and the presentation was a disaster! My hands were shaking, and I couldn’t remember half of what I wanted to say. Mr. Dube looked a little disappointed. I felt terrible. Why didn’t I just stop for a minute and check myself? It’s like, I was so focused on the kids, I forgot about me.

[REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] Nomusa at the clinic told me a lot of things. She said my blood sugar was a little high, and that eating too much of the sugary things from the tuck shop was making it worse. She showed me pictures of good foods – lots of vegetables, like spinach and cabbage, and fruits like apples and bananas. She said I could have porridge with milk instead of just sadza, and that it would help keep my energy up. She also gave me a little booklet with recipes – simple things, like a bean stew and a carrot and tomato soup. It felt a bit strange, trying to change my eating habits. I still wanted my bunny chow sometimes! But she said, ‘Participant, you need to think about the school presentation, and all the other things you need to do. You need to be strong.’

I tried making the bean stew last night. It wasn’t as good as my mama’s, but it was still tasty. I even ate some of the carrots and tomatoes! And today, I actually checked my blood sugar before lunch. It was a little lower than yesterday. Mr. Dube noticed my presentation was better – much better! He said he was proud of my effort. It felt good to have done well, and it made me want to keep trying. I’m going to try to eat a bit healthier every day, just like [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] Nomusa said. Maybe tomorrow, I'll even make a big pot of porridge. It's a slow change, but it feels good. I’m starting to realize that taking care of myself is just as important as teaching my kids.

input.story:
My name is Participant, and I teach young ones here in Dispatch. It’s a busy life, you know? I live in a little house near the market, not fancy, but it’s home. My days are full – lesson plans, making sure the children eat, and then helping my mama with the garden. We mostly eat what we can grow: maize porridge for breakfast, sometimes a bit of cabbage if we’re lucky, and a meaty stew for supper. I take my insulin and my pills, like I’m supposed to, but sometimes, I just…forget. It’s easy to do, isn’t it?  Do you ever just get so busy you forget to take care of yourself?  I was grading papers yesterday, a big stack of them, and I just kept eating biscuits. I felt a bit tired, but I told myself it was just the heat.  Then, my head started to feel funny, and I had to sit down.  It was a proper struggle to finish the lesson, and the children looked a bit confused. It made me think, maybe I need to pay more attention to what my body is telling me.

Today, I had to go to the clinic. Mr. Participant, the [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], he’s a good man. He always asks about my blood sugar, and he tells me to walk a little bit every day. He says it helps with the sugar, and keeps my heart strong. I told him I don’t have time, that teaching takes up all my days. He just smiled and said, ‘Participant, your health is like a small seed. If you don’t water it, it won't grow.  Just a little bit each day, that’s all it takes.’ He gave me a pamphlet with pictures of healthy food – bright red tomatoes, green beans, and lovely oranges.  I took it home, but honestly, I just put it on the table and forgot about it. My mama was making umleqiso, and I was hungry, so I had a piece of that, too. It’s hard to change, you know? Especially when you're used to things one way.

I tried to walk today, like Mr. Participant said. I started slowly, just around the yard. But then, my sister, Thandi, she called and asked me to help her with the laundry.  It's always something! So, I folded clothes for a good hour, and by the time I finished, I felt really tired. My feet were aching, and I forgot all about my walk.  I told myself, ‘Tomorrow, tomorrow,’ but then I started planning the next day’s lessons.  It’s like, my job is important, and my family needs me, so I just keep going, keep going. But I know, deep down, that if I don’t take care of myself, I won’t be able to do anything for anyone. My boss, Mr. Nkosi, he's expecting a big report next week, and I need to be sharp to finish it.

Today, I walked for fifteen minutes, just after my lesson. It wasn't much, but it felt good. I even ate an orange, a real juicy one!  Mr. Participant will be pleased. The report for Mr. Nkosi? I finished it, and it was good, really good. I didn’t feel that funny head, and I had plenty of energy. I’m starting to see that taking care of myself isn’t just about medicine; it’s about being strong for my family and for my work.  It’s like planting that little seed – a little bit of water, a little bit of sunshine, and it grows.  And maybe, just maybe, I’ll even have time to dance a little umxhentso with my grandchildren soon.

input.story:
My name is Participant, and I’m fifty-eight. I work at the market, selling vegetables. It’s honest work, but it’s tiring, you know? Most days, I eat pap and beans – that’s all I can really afford. Sometimes, if I’ve got a good day, I’ll add a bit of meat, maybe some mielie. It keeps me going. But I don't really think much about *why* I need to be strong, you know? It just… is.  Didn’t always feel this tired, though. I used to love dancing, umxhentso, really get my energy out.  But lately, my legs ache something fierce after just a few stalls. I just brush it off, say it's old age.  Do you think it’s just old age, really?

Yesterday, I was helping Mr. Nkosi load his truck – he’s a carpenter, a good man. He needed a strong back to lift a big piece of wood. I tried to help, but my legs just wouldn’t cooperate. I stumbled, and the wood fell, nearly hitting him! Mr. Nkosi was so worried. He said, ‘Participant, you need to take care of yourself. You’re not getting any younger.’  It made me feel a bit silly, I must admit. I just shook my head and mumbled something about being tired. It was a small thing, but it made me realize something. Maybe he was right.  I need to listen to my body, but it's hard, isn't it?

Today, I went to the clinic. It wasn’t fancy, just a small building near the hospital, but the [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], Miss Zola, was kind. She checked my blood pressure – it was a bit high, she said. She told me about eating healthy, about fruits and vegetables. She said things like, ‘Pap and beans are good, Participant, but you need more colour in your plate.’ She gave me a little booklet with simple recipes – things like spinach and tomato stew, and butternut squash.  It sounded… complicated.  And expensive! I asked her about traditional foods, like umdibi, and she said, ‘You can still have umdibi, but maybe just a little bit, and with a side of something healthy.’ It felt like a lot to think about.  I just nodded and thanked her, feeling a bit lost, to be honest.

I tried making the stew today. It was okay. Not brilliant

input.story:
My name is Participant, and I run a little shop selling spices and herbs down in Khayelitsha. It’s a good life, you know? Lots of people come to me for good ingredients. But lately, my legs have been feeling funny, like they’re tired all the time. I just put it down to being busy, always running around, shouting at the delivery guys, and making sure I have enough stock. I eat what I can – sometimes a quick braai, sometimes just some pap and beans. It’s easy to grab something quick when you’re busy, isn’t it? I don't really think about how it’s affecting me, you know? Just get on with things.  Yesterday, I was trying to unload a big crate of turmeric, and I nearly tripped! It was embarrassing, and I had to ask Thando, my assistant, to help me. It made me think, ‘Participant, you need to take care of yourself, man!’

The clinic down the road, the one Dr. Zola runs, it’s a proper place. Clean, bright, and everyone is nice. I went in because my sister, Nomusa, she’s always telling me to get checked. I wasn’t sure why, honestly. I thought it was just an old man’s thing. But Dr. Zola looked at me and said, ‘Participant, your blood sugar is a bit high. You need to start moving more, and eat a bit lighter.’ He gave me a little card with some pictures – fruits and vegetables, things like that. He said, ‘Even a short walk every day can make a big difference.’ It sounded a bit scary, to be honest. Walking? I’m used to running around my shop all day! But he said it's important, and he seemed like a good man. He told me to take my insulin properly and to talk to my pharmacist about my medication.  It felt… a little overwhelming, to be honest.

I tried walking, I really did. I started with just ten minutes after closing up the shop. It felt so hard! My legs still ached, and I kept wanting to just sit down and have a cold drink. Then, my cousin, Siyabonga, he’s a fitness trainer, he saw me struggling. He said, ‘Participant, you gotta push yourself! Think about the big order coming in next week – Mr. Nkosi wants a huge shipment of chilli peppers. You need to be strong enough to carry those crates!’ That helped a little. But then I had a lekker biltong sandwich for lunch, and my legs felt even worse.  It’s so hard to change, you know?  Everything feels easier when you’re tired. I almost gave up, but I kept thinking about Mr. Nkosi and those chilli peppers.  It's a big order, and I need to be able to handle it.

Slowly, though, things started to feel a bit better. I started taking little walks during my lunch break, just around the shop. I even started adding a few more vegetables to my meals – some spinach in my pap, a bit of tomato with my braai. And guess what? I managed to carry those chilli peppers to Mr. Nkosi without even thinking about my legs! He was really pleased, and I felt proud of myself. It wasn’t easy, but I did it. I think I'm starting to understand that taking care of myself isn’t just about being strong for work; it’s about feeling good, about being able to enjoy life.  And you know what?  I’m even thinking about maybe joining that traditional dancing group down the street. It might be a good way to get some exercise, and it would be fun too!

input.story:
Hayi, life as a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] is busy, neh? Every day is a hustle, trying to get everything done. I love my job at the school in East London, but honestly, by the time I get home, I'm just tired. I try to eat properly, you know, a nice pot of umngqusho with some chicken, or maybe some fish braaied on the weekend. But sometimes, after marking all those tests, I just crave something sweet. A little koeksister with my tea, maybe? Or a slice of cake my neighbour brings over. It’s just a small thing, a little treat before bed. Last week, I was supposed to prepare the class attendance report for the principal first thing on Monday morning. I stayed up late finishing it, had a little something sweet with my tea, and then…well, I couldn’t even focus on the report in the morning. My head was fuzzy, and I kept making mistakes. It took me almost the whole day to fix it, and the principal wasn't impressed. I just thought I was tired, but maybe…maybe it was something else.

My sister, Nombulelo, she’s a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], she noticed I was always a bit sluggish in the mornings. She told me, ‘Participant, you need to go to the clinic. You’ve been diagnosed with diabetes, you need to get it checked.’ I was a little scared, to be honest. I thought diabetes was something old people got. But Nombulelo insisted, and she even came with me to the clinic. The sister there, Sister Thandiwe, was so kind. She explained that eating late, especially sweet things, can mess with my blood sugar. She showed me how my body uses sugar, and how too much at night makes it hard for my body to cope while I’m sleeping. She said I should try a small handful of nuts or some Greek yogurt if I’m really hungry, instead of the sweet things. She even wrote down a few easy snack ideas for me, and told me to check with her again in a month. She said, ‘It's not about stopping everything you enjoy, Participant, it’s about finding a balance.’ It made sense, but it still felt…difficult.

Okay, so I tried the nuts. It’s not the same as a koeksister, let me tell you! The first few nights were hard. I kept wanting something sweet, and I’d end up sneaking a biscuit or two. Then I remembered the school play was coming up. I was in charge of organizing the costumes, a big job with lots of parents and kids involved. If I was tired and unfocused, it would be a disaster. So I really tried. I started having a small apple with a little peanut butter before bed instead. Some nights I failed, and had a small piece of chocolate, but I tried to make up for it the next day with a walk after school. It wasn't easy, my body was used to that sugar. But I kept telling myself, 'You need to be sharp for the play, Participant!'

Slowly, things started to change. I wasn't as tired in the mornings anymore. I could actually concentrate on the attendance reports without getting a headache. The school play went off without a hitch – the costumes were perfect, everything ran smoothly. Even the principal complimented me! And you know what? I started *enjoying* the apple and peanut butter. It felt good to take care of myself. Sister Thandiwe was pleased when I went back for my check-up. My blood sugar was better, and I felt better. I still have a sweet tooth, but now I understand it’s okay to have a little treat sometimes, just not right before bed. Nombulelo keeps encouraging me to join her for walks, and I think I will. Maybe I’ll even try some of those traditional games we used to play as children. It feels good to be in control, and to know that taking care of my health will help me be the best [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] I can be.

Eish, life, neh? I’m Participant, and I’ve been a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] for… well, too many years to count now! [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], but still helping out at the school with marking papers, you see. It’s good to keep busy. I like my routine. Strong tea in the morning, always with a biscuit – a nice sweet one. Lunch is usually umngqusho, because it reminds me of my mother. And a cigarette with it, of course. Don’t tell anyone, but I still enjoy a little tot of umqombothi with friends on weekends. Yesterday, the headmistress asked me to check all the Grade 7 exam papers for maths. Simple enough, I thought. But after a few papers, my eyes… they just blurred. I couldn’t see the numbers properly. Had to ask my neighbour’s daughter to help finish. Shameful, really. I thought my eyes were just getting old, but maybe… maybe it's something else?

Old Man Ndlovu, the clinic [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], he’s a good man. I went to see him about my blurry vision, and he checked everything. Blood pressure, sugar levels… the works. Turns out, my sugar was high. Very high. He said it’s the diabetes, and it's affecting my eyes. 'Participant,' he said, 'you need to watch what you eat, and you *need* to stop smoking. It’s making everything worse.' I told him, 'But I enjoy my tea and biscuit! And the cigarette calms my nerves!' He smiled, a kind smile. 'I understand, Mama Participant. But small changes. Start with cutting down on sugar in your tea. Walk for 30 minutes every day. And try to reduce the cigarettes, even just one less a day. Think of your eyes, and those Grade 7 papers you need to mark!' It sounded… doable. But still, it felt like a lot to change.

This walking, it’s harder than it looks! I tried to walk to the shop yesterday, but my feet started aching after just ten minutes. And the biscuit… oh, the biscuit! I tried drinking my tea without it, but it felt… empty. I ended up having one anyway. Just one, I told myself. Then I remembered those exam papers, and the headmistress relying on me. I can't let her down. So, I forced myself to walk a little further today, even though my feet complained. I walked to Mrs. Participant’s house and back, and we chatted for a while. It was nice. I even managed to drink my tea with just a little sugar. It wasn’t the same, but it wasn’t terrible. I still had a cigarette, though. Baby steps, I suppose. It's a struggle, this changing habits, but I need to be able to see those numbers!

It’s been a week now, and things are… better. I’m walking for twenty minutes every day, and I’ve swapped the sweet biscuits for a small handful of nuts. I still have my tea, but with just half a teaspoon of sugar. And I’ve cut down to five cigarettes a day, instead of ten. My eyes aren’t blurry all the time anymore. Amazing, really. Today, I marked all the Grade 7 exam papers myself, without needing any help! I even double-checked them. I felt… proud. Old Man Ndlovu was pleased when I told him. He said I was doing well, and to keep it up. I’m starting to think maybe he’s right. Maybe taking care of myself isn’t so bad after all. Perhaps I'll even join that gospel choir at the church. It would be good to sing again, and maybe… maybe I’ll learn some new healthy recipes too. Who knows what else I can achieve if I just take things one step at a time?

input.story:
Hayi, life, it keeps moving, doesn't it? I'm Participant, and I work as an [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] at the hospital here in East London. It’s busy, always papers to sort, files to check. I love my job, but sometimes… sometimes my head just feels foggy. I usually start my day with a strong cup of tea and a vetkoek from Mama Nomsa’s stall down the road – so warm and tasty! And lunch? Usually a bunny chow, nice and filling. It’s quick, you see. I don’t have time to fuss with fancy food. Yesterday, I was supposed to prepare the patient admission reports for Dr. Ndlovu. Simple enough, right? But my mind just wouldn’t focus. I kept making mistakes, dates wrong, names misspelled. Dr. Ndlovu wasn’t happy, not at all. I just felt… sluggish, like my brain was swimming in mielie-meal.

I eventually went to the clinic, feeling a bit silly, to be honest. I thought, 'What can a doctor do about a foggy brain?' But Sister Thandi was very kind. She explained about my sugar, how the vetkoek and bunny chow, as delicious as they are, can make it go up and down. She said that's why I was feeling tired and struggling to concentrate. 'Participant,' she said, 'your body is like a car. You need the right fuel to make it run smoothly.' She showed me a list of foods - lots of greens, beans, some fruit, and even a little bit of brown rice. She said I could still have my tea, just not so much sugar. It sounded…different. A little bit difficult, maybe. But Dr. Ndlovu is giving me a big project next month, a whole new patient tracking system to set up. I *need* to be sharp for that.

Trying to change things has been… a bit of a battle, I won't lie. Yesterday, I promised myself a salad for lunch, but the smell of the fish and chips from the takeaway next door… oh, it was strong! I ended up grabbing a small portion, telling myself it wouldn’t hurt. And it did, a little. I felt that sluggishness creep back in the afternoon. But I remembered the patient tracking system. I pictured myself, confident and organized, presenting it to Dr. Ndlovu. That thought pushed me to make a proper dinner - some spinach and beans with a little bit of butternut squash. It wasn't a vetkoek, but it wasn’t bad. I even danced a little umxhentso in the kitchen while I cooked, to keep my spirits up. 

Slowly, things are getting easier. I’ve started swapping my tea for herbal infusions and having a small piece of fruit instead of a vetkoek. I'm still having my tea, but with just a tiny bit of sugar. The brain fog is lifting, bit by bit. And you know what? I actually *enjoy* the new foods! Mama Nomsa even started making a spinach and bean pie for me, she said she wants me to be healthy. Last week, I finished the first draft of the patient tracking system, and Dr. Ndlovu was impressed! She said it was well-organized and easy to understand. I felt so proud. Maybe taking care of my body isn't just about feeling good, maybe it's about being able to do the things I love, and do them well. Now, I’m thinking… what else can I change to feel even better?

It’s a good job, I love the children, but sometimes… sometimes it’s hard to keep up! I always feel tired, you see? And I like a little something sweet with my tea, maybe a biscuit or two, or even a nice piece of koeksister after supper. It just helps me relax after a long day of marking papers and trying to get little ones to understand their numbers. Last week, I promised to help Miss Participant with the school play decorations, painting all the backdrop scenes. I thought, easy peasy! But halfway through, I felt so weak and shaky, I had to stop. I just sat there, staring at the half-finished tree, wondering what was wrong with me. It was embarrassing, really. What good is a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] who can't even paint a tree?

My neighbour, Mama Nomusa, she noticed I was looking a bit down. She’s like my second mother, always looking out for me. She told me I should go to the clinic, just to check things. I wasn’t keen, honestly. Clinics, they always make you wait, and I thought, I’m just a little tired. But Mama Nomusa, she insisted. So I went. The sister, she was very kind. She checked my blood sugar and explained that my sweet tooth was causing trouble. She said I have something called ‘diabetes’ and that I need to watch what I eat. ‘Participant,’ she said, ‘you need to swap those biscuits for something healthier. A handful of peanuts, maybe, or a piece of fruit. And don’t wait until you’re starving to eat, have small snacks throughout the day.’ She even gave me a list of foods I could eat and told me about [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] options. It sounded… different. But she explained it would help me have more energy for my work, and for my children at school. Maybe she was right.

Trying to change my habits wasn't easy, I tell you! I'm used to my tea and biscuits, it’s a comfort. The first few days, I kept forgetting to pack the peanuts, and then I’d end up grabbing a biscuit from the shop anyway. One afternoon, I was supposed to meet with another [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] to plan a lesson, and I completely forgot my snack. I felt so grumpy and couldn’t concentrate. But then I remembered the school play decorations. Miss Participant was counting on me! I couldn’t let her down again. So I quickly ran to the shop and bought an apple. It wasn't a koeksister, but it helped a little. It’s a slow process, this changing, but I knew I had to keep trying. It’s like learning a new izibongo – it takes practice.

Slowly, slowly, things started to get better. I started packing a small bag with apples, peanuts, and sometimes even biltong for a protein boost. I still have my tea, but without the mountains of sugar. And you know what? I started feeling stronger! I finished the backdrop for the school play, the tree looks beautiful, and Miss Participant was so pleased. I even had enough energy to help with the costumes. I still get cravings for something sweet, but now I can usually resist. The sister at the clinic said I need to keep checking my blood sugar, and I am. It’s not perfect, but I’m learning. I’m starting to think maybe, just maybe, taking care of myself isn’t so bad after all. Maybe it’s even… a good thing. Who knew a little change in my snacks could make such a big difference?

input.story:
Hayi, life as a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] in this village, it keeps you on your toes, doesn't it? Every morning, it's straight to school, helping the little ones with their numbers and letters. I love my job, truly. But lately, I've been feeling… sluggish. Just tired, you know? Breakfast is usually a piece of kota with polony – quick and easy. Lunch? Often a pap and chakalaka from the shebeen across the road. It fills you up, and it’s cheap. Yesterday, I promised to help Old Man Themba mend the fence around the school veggie garden before the parents arrived for the meeting. I figured, easy enough. But after just a few poles, I was completely out of breath, leaning on the fence itself! Honestly, it was embarrassing. I had to ask young Participant to finish it for me. What does it say about me, if I can’t even fix a fence?

I felt so ashamed after that fence business, I finally went to the clinic. Sister Nandi, she's a good woman. She checked my sugar, and well, it wasn’t looking good. She explained about the diabetes, how the sweet things and not moving enough were causing problems. I told her, 'But Sister Nandi, kota is life! And I don’t have time for fancy exercise!' She just smiled gently. She said, ‘Participant, we’re not asking you to run a marathon. Just a little walk each day, maybe around the village. And instead of polony every day, try adding some beans or eggs to your kota. Small changes, that’s all.’ She even showed me some simple stretches I could do while I'm marking papers. It sounded…doable, I guess. Still, it felt like a lot to think about.

Trying to walk every day is harder than it looks! I started, I really did. But the first few days, my legs felt like lead. And the kota… oh, the kota! It calls to me! I slipped up on Tuesday and had a double polony kota, and the next day I felt even worse than usual. My feet were aching, and I felt so frustrated. But then I remembered the school play. We’re preparing the children for the Heritage Day celebrations, and I’m supposed to choreograph the umxhentso dance. If I can't even keep up with a simple walk, how am I going to teach those energetic little ones a whole dance routine? That thought pushed me to get moving again, even if it was just a slow walk around the school grounds.

Slowly, things started to change. I started adding beans to my kota most days, and I even tried making a simple vegetable stew a couple of times. The walking got easier, and I started feeling…lighter, somehow. I even managed to do a few of Sister Nandi’s stretches while watching TV. The day of the school play arrived, and I was nervous, but I wasn’t breathless. I danced with the children, showing them the steps, and I didn’t have to stop and catch my breath once! The parents were so impressed, and Old Man Themba winked at me. It felt good, really good. Maybe, just maybe, taking care of myself isn’t so hard after all. Maybe I can even learn to enjoy it. And who knows, maybe next year I'll be able to fix that fence all by myself.

Hayi, life is busy, neh? I’m Participant, and I work at the taxi rank, selling vetkoek and chips. It's hard work, standing all day, and the smell of the oil… well, it sticks to you. I love my work, it puts food on the table, but lately, I’ve been feeling… sluggish. Like my legs are made of lead after a long day. I usually grab a kota for lunch – quick and easy! – and maybe a cool drink. Last week, Old Man Participant asked me to count all the money from the day, a big job he usually does. I was so tired, my head was spinning, and I messed up the counting! He wasn’t happy. He said, 'Participant, you need to focus!' But how can I focus when my body feels like it’s fighting me?

I went to the clinic, you know, just to check. [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] Zanele, she’s a good woman, looked at my file and said, ‘Participant, your sugar is a little high.’ Sugar? I thought that was just for sweet things! She explained about how vetkoek and kota, even though they taste good, can make things tricky. She said I needed to eat more greens, more beans, and less oil. 'It doesn’t mean you can’t enjoy your food, just… a little bit different,' she said. She gave me a list of cheap, healthy foods – spinach, lentils, sweet potatoes. Honestly, I was a bit skeptical. Could I really feel better just by changing what I eat? It sounded… difficult.

Okay, so I tried. I really did. I swapped some of the vetkoek dough for mashed sweet potato, hoping to make them a bit healthier. But the first batch? They tasted like… nothing! My customers weren’t impressed. I almost gave up. Then I remembered Old Man Participant is trusting me with the end-of-month takings soon. A much bigger job! If I messed that up, I could lose my job. So, I tried again. This time, I mixed the sweet potato with a little butternut squash, and added some spices. Better! Still not perfect, but better. It's hard, changing what you've always done, you know? But I had to try.

Slowly, things started to change. I started adding a side of chakalaka – tomato and bean relish – to the plates. It’s cheap, it’s tasty, and it fills people up. I even started drinking more water instead of those sugary drinks. And you know what? I *felt* better. Not right away, but after a few weeks, my legs didn't ache so much. When I counted Old Man Participant’s money at the end of the month, I didn’t make a single mistake! He smiled, a real smile, and said, ‘See, Participant? Focus comes with a clear head.’ Maybe [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] Zanele was right. Maybe eating healthy isn’t just about feeling good, it’s about being able to *do* good, too. I'm still learning, but now I think, maybe, just maybe, I can enjoy my food *and* take care of myself.

At first, I was a bit resistant, thinking that I didn't have time for this, but Sister Nomsa assured me that even small changes could make a big difference. input.story:
I wake up every morning, feeling a bit tired, but I have to get ready for my traditional dancing practice. I love dancing, it's my hobby, and it makes me feel alive. After practice, I usually grab something quick to eat, like a vetkoek or a bunny chow, and then I'm off to my daily chores. I never really thought about how my diet and lack of exercise could affect my energy levels and my work. But today, I had a small task to do, which was to help my friend with her stall at the market. I was so tired that I had to take a break, and I ended up not finishing the task. I thought to myself, "What's wrong with me? Why am I so tired all the time?" 

I decided to visit my local healthcare clinic to get some advice. The healthcare worker, Sister Ntombi, was very helpful and explained to me that my diet and lack of exercise were affecting my energy levels. She told me that I need to start taking care of my health, especially since I have Type 2 Diabetes. She advised me to start walking every day and to eat more balanced meals. I was a bit resistant at first, I didn't know if I could do it, but Sister Ntombi reassured me that it's all about making small changes and that she would be there to support me. She also reminded me that my traditional dancing can be a great way to get exercise, so I should keep doing that.

I started taking Sister Ntombi's advice, but it wasn't easy. I had to adjust my routine, and it was hard to get used to walking every day. I also had to change my diet, which was difficult because I love my traditional foods. But I knew I had to do it, especially since I have a bigger task coming up, which is to perform at the annual cultural festival. I didn't want to be too tired to dance, so I persisted. However, I did have a minor setback when I forgot to take my medication one day, and I had to remind myself to take it. But I didn't give up, I kept going, and I started to feel a bit better.

It's been a few weeks now, and I can see the improvement in my health. I have more energy, and I can dance for longer without getting tired. I'm also eating more balanced meals, and I've started to enjoy my daily walks. The festival is approaching, and I'm feeling more confident about my performance. I realize now that taking care of my health is not just about me, it's also about being able to do the things I love, like dancing. I'm grateful for Sister Ntombi's advice, and I'm open to continuing to make healthy changes in my life.

input.story:
You know, I often find myself snacking late at night after studying or hanging out with my family. I used to think, 'It's just a little food, it won't matter much.' But one night, after eating some leftover pap and fried chicken at 10 PM, I woke up feeling dizzy and tired. I thought, 'Am I just tired from late nights, or is it something else?' It felt like my blood sugar was acting up, but I didn't really connect the dots. I tried to push through schoolwork and family plans, but I was drained. How was I supposed to focus on my studies and help with family celebrations if my body was like this?"

I decided to go to the local clinic for some help, where the sister explained things clearly. She said eating late at night can cause your blood sugar to spike because your body isn't as active to use the energy. She told me that instead of big late meals, I could try lighter snacks like a small fruit or some nuts, and to avoid heavy foods close to bedtime. She also reminded me to keep up my insulin on time and encouraged me to walk more—like brisk walks around the neighborhood, about 30 minutes, five days a week. It sounded doable but also different from my usual routine. I felt a bit unsure but wanted to try it for my health and also to feel better at school and home."

The next few days, I tried to eat smaller meals earlier in the evening and go for walks after class. But sometimes, I got hungry late and reached for sweets or leftover food again because it was easy and comforting after a long day. One evening, I felt a bit shaky and realized my blood sugar had gone high. I felt frustrated with myself and wondered if I could keep this up. But then I remembered the big family gathering coming up next month where I wanted to enjoy the food and have energy to dance and laugh with everyone. That gave me reason to keep trying, even if I stumbled a little now and then."

input.question: [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
You know, every morning I push myself to the market, standing long hours, selling things, thinking that’s enough exercise, right? But then I start feeling tired, and my sugar levels go all over the place. One day, I was asked by my boss to help carry heavy boxes early in the morning, and I nearly had to stop. I thought, 'Is this how my body wants to behave?' I hadn’t really thought much about the kind of exercise that would be good for me. I just moved as I always did, thinking that was enough for diabetes. Turns out, it wasn’t, and I struggled to finish that small task. I guess I was missing something important about taking care of my body for work."

Then I went to my regular check-up at the local clinic, telling the [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] about my tiredness and trouble with the boxes. She smiled kindly and said, ‘Participant, exercising doesn’t have to be hard or heavy. Walking for 30 minutes, gentle dancing like our umxhentso, or even stretching can help keep your blood sugar steady.’ I wasn’t sure at first, thinking, ‘Can dancing really be exercise for my diabetes?’ But she explained how moving your body helps insulin work better, and how it fits nicely with our own culture. She even said to start slow and listen to my body. That advice sounded doable and made me feel hopeful.”

So I started trying — a little walk here, a few dance steps there. But, oh, it was tough changing old habits. Sometimes I forgot or felt lazy after a long day at the market. There was a day when my sugar dropped a bit too low because I walked too fast without eating properly first. That scared me a bit, and I almost gave up. But I remembered there’s a bigger task coming up — a community festival where I’d join the dance group to celebrate our culture. I wanted to be strong for that day, so I kept going, learning bit by bit how to balance rest, food, and movement."

Now, I feel a little lighter and more able to carry my things at work without feeling drained. The festival came, and I danced with joy, not worrying about my sugar spikes or crashes. I learned that small, safe exercises can make a real difference, and I’m even planning to keep it up because it helps me with my diabetes and my spirit. Who would have thought that embracing our traditional dances and easy walks would give me not just strength, but more hope and happiness? I’m ready for whatever comes next, knowing I can take care of myself while doing what I love."

You know, it wasn't so long ago when I thought a bit of rest was best for me, especially with this diabetes and high blood pressure. I still had my old habits – sitting most of the day, eating the same foods, and hardly moving around much. When a little chore came up at the house – like fetching firewood or helping a neighbour – I’d feel tired quickly. I blamed my age, but maybe I didn’t see how my health was getting the better of me. It was like my body didn’t want to play along, and I was missing the signs. Do we sometimes forget just how much our bodies tell us, if only we listen?"

One day at the clinic, [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] Thandi helped me understand a bit more about moving safely with diabetes. At first, I was unsure – ‘How can a person my age start exercising without overdoing it?’ I asked. She gently explained that walking slowly, doing some traditional dance moves like umxhentso, and even light stretching are good ways to start. She said these exercises help lower blood sugar and keep our hearts strong, which is great for hypertension too. Best part, she told me to listen to my body and stop if I felt pain. Sometimes, I forget to check my blood sugar. My mind’s already in the classroom—marking, sorting lessons, keeping order. Last week, on Monday morning, I had to run a reading circle with the grade sixes. But halfway through, I started feeling a bit dizzy. Maybe it was the bread, maybe I skipped my medicine. I pushed myself to keep going though, thinking, 'Strong men finish what they start, right?' But the lesson didn’t go as planned. I fumbled with my words, and the kids could see I wasn’t myself. I felt so embarrassed that I wanted to hide. Who knew food and medicine could make my work so tough?

Later that day, I went to the local clinic, just down the road. The [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] there, Sister Zama, saw me looking tired. She called me in with a gentle voice, 'Bhuti Participant, let’s talk.' I told her how I didn’t understand which meals were best or if a bit of imifino now and then was enough. She nodded and said, 'No need for shame. Try umngqusho (samp and beans), imifino, and roasted sweet potatoes. Don’t use too much salt, and check that you are eating breakfast—with soft porridge, not white bread.' She drew me a simple menu in isiXhosa and English, then smiled and added, 'Next time, pack a small apple and water for your break. And don’t forget your medicine.'

The next morning, I tried Sister Zama’s suggestions. I made soft sorghum porridge, added a little milk, and packed leftover umngqusho for lunch. At first, it felt strange, you know? My friends in the staffroom teased me, 'Participant, where’s your vetkoek?' But I remembered my big storytelling event was coming up, and I wanted to be sharp. That day, I accidentally left my apple at home and felt hungry before my next class. I started doubting myself, but I remembered why I was doing this. I wanted to perform well at the festival, not just survive the day.

Over the next week, I got used to my new routine. My sugar stopped jumping up and down, and I had more energy in the classroom. On Saturday, I stood in front of a full hall for my praise poetry session. My voice was strong. I remembered every line. Afterwards, my friends hugged me, saying, 'You look good, bhuti!' I smiled, thinking how a little change in my meals gave me back so much confidence. Now, I want to keep learning new ways to live healthier, not just for work, but for all the tomorrows ahead.

input.question: [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
My name is Participant and you know, I always wake up before dawn, make a quick cup of tea, and rush to school with nothing but a white bread sandwich in my bag. Sometimes I eat fried chips from the street vendor or a cheap magwinya during break, because who has time, neh? I was feeling a bit dizzy, but I decided I must mark my class tests before the bell rings. But eish, my hands shook so much I scribbled by mistake and had to redo everything. Don't you hate when you want to work hard but your own body just doesn't listen?

Later that day, Sister Zinzi, the [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] from the clinic, caught me while I was leaving the staff room. She smiled and greeted, 'Participant, sisi, can we talk quick-quick about your sugar?' At first, I felt tired and did not want another lecture. But she didn't judge me, just asked, 'What do you usually eat at school?' When I answered, she shook her head gently and told me, 'Next time, try umngqusho or umfino—samp and beans, or maize meal with spinach. Bring those from home in a lunchbox, you’ll see. They keep your energy and won’t spike your sugar. And if you feel tired, take a short walk.’ Simple advice, but I still was not sure it would really help.

The next morning, I packed umfino and chakalaka for lunch like she said, but I missed my magwinya already—these food changes feel strange, qha! After my first class, my hands reached for the old sugar doughnut in my drawer, then I remembered Sister Zinzi’s words. Heh, this healthy routine is difficult, but I have to try. The headmaster gave me news: I must lead the school play next week, so I need my strength. I didn't want to let anyone see me failing again.

Day by day, as I kept bringing my home-packed foods and snuck in a few dizzying dance steps during breaks, things got better. I had more energy to practise umxhentso with the girls for the big Friday. Even when I wanted to give up, I thought of all the children counting on me. By opening my lunchbox and feeling strong, I finished marking test scripts and even got compliments from the headmaster. Now, when Sister Zinzi greets me, I laugh and say, ‘Sisi, your umfino advice is working. Maybe I can change, step by step.’

input.question: [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]
input.story:
Some mornings, I wake up early and smell tea brewing in my own kitchen. I pack my lunch—rice with chicken stew, and sometimes an apple if I remember. I give myself an insulin injection and swallow my other medication with water. These things are like brushing my teeth, neh? Sometimes, I don’t even think about what they do. That morning, I was preparing lesson plans for my Grade 4’s, hoping to finish the handouts before school so I don’t have to worry later. Suddenly, halfway into my planning, my hands started to shake, and I felt tired, but I ignored it, thinking, 'Maybe I’m just hungry? Should I push through?' I told myself to finish the simple handout task quickly, but I ended up forgetting some important things, and my head just couldn’t work right. That small task became a mess. How am I supposed to teach when I feel so tired?

Later, I went to the local clinic near my school. The [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] called me in, saying, 'Participant, are you alright?' I tried to explain, but she seemed to just know I was struggling with my sugar and my busy routine. She smiled gently and said, 'Take it slow, sisi. Try walking even just ten minutes before work. It helps your sugar, and makes you feel stronger for your learners.' Part of me wanted to argue, because who has time? But I nodded, because the [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] seemed to understand exactly how tired teachers always feel. I needed simple advice, not a big lecture. She wrote a small plan for me—'Start with one walk, then see if your handouts go better.' I thought, 'Maybe, just maybe, I can try.'

The next morning, I put on my sweatpants and walked down my quiet street before sunrise. Ai, the first five minutes, I wanted to turn back. My legs felt heavy, and I kept thinking of all the work waiting. I worried, was this really going to help? I almost skipped my walk, but remembered I have to help plan the school’s Heritage Day celebration—it’s a big job! I told myself, 'If I can do this small walk, maybe I’ll have energy for my learners and the big event.' I finished my walk slowly, feeling a little proud. Did I fix everything? Not yet, but I tried.

Over the next few weeks, my short walks slowly turned into a normal thing. My mornings didn’t feel so hard, and my lesson handouts made more sense. The Heritage Day event came, and as I handed out prizes to the best-dressed learners, I realised, 'Hey, I didn’t feel so tired this year.' My principal even smiled and said, 'Well done, Participant!' I know I still get discouraged sometimes, but now I understand: just starting with one small change can help me and my learners. Maybe next time, I won’t wait until I’m tired to look after myself.

Usually, I like to snack while I work, so I grabbed amagwinya and sweet rooibos tea, thinking it would help me focus. As I worked on the lesson outline, my eyes started feeling heavy, and I just felt tired. Can you imagine? I couldn’t even finish my class poster! I wondered, 'Is this from age, or maybe from the food I ate?' I just didn’t know which foods were good for my sugar.

Later in the week, I went to our local clinic for my regular check-up. The [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], Sister Zanele, noticed my blood sugar was a bit high and asked about my meals. I told her about my snacking. She gave me friendly advice, saying, 'Mama Participant, rather try snacking on things like unsalted nuts, fresh fruit like apples, and wholegrain crackers. These won’t spike your sugar too much. Also, small portions are best—don’t eat all at once. You’ll have more energy at work and for your dancing!' I wanted to argue, but honestly, who am I to question a [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] who knows these things?

That night, I packed a small container of apple slices and a handful of peanuts to take to class the next day. Eish, old habits die hard! I found myself craving something sweet during my tea break, and I almost reached for a scone in the staffroom. But I remembered, next week was the big parent-[REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] meeting, and I needed all my energy. Holding my apple, I sighed, and took a slow bite instead. Was this really going to help?

By the time the meeting came, I had stuck to my new snacks for a week. I didn’t get tired, not even once! I stood up in front of all the parents, speaking with confidence and answering questions. I even planned a small dance with the learners afterward. Now I see—changing a snack isn’t so hard if you decide to try, especially when you notice the difference. I’m ready to learn more step by step. Who says old ladies can’t change?

That morning, I was unpacking a delivery, and I felt heavy, my legs like bricks and my eyes blurry. I pushed myself to finish, but then boom, I dropped a whole carton of bottles. My boss shook his head, aaai Participant, but he asked if I was okay. I just wiped my face and said, "Ja, just tired." Deep down, I wondered, "Is it really just tired, or is something wrong? Maybe my blood sugar again?" But I didn’t know, so after mopping the mess, I just grabbed a cheap samoosa and a fizzy drink for lunch like always.

Later, after work, I went to the clinic because my body was still feeling weird. The [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] there sat me down and asked about what I eat. She looked at me with those kind eyes and said, "Participant, you must try to swap that soda for water and eat brown bread instead of white. Put maybe some beans, cabbage, and chicken (not fried) in your lunch box. Even if you don’t have much, these foods are right at home, and they won’t push your sugar up and down like a minibus taxi on the highway, you know?" I almost laughed at her example but felt shy too. Can eating these simple things really help?

So, the next day, I tried the [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]’s advice. My lunch was brown bread, baked beans, and a bottle of water. Yoh, it felt odd, hey. No Coke, no chips. My friend Participant even joked, 'Participant, are you on a diet now?' It wasn’t easy, and I kept thinking about that big stock take coming next week. I nearly gave up and bought a koeksister, but I thought, 'Let me give these small changes a chance.' The [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE] said it might help, so why not, neh?

A week later, the stock take came. This time, I felt lighter and clearer. My hands didn’t shake, no blurry eyes—nothing. I worked fast, kept cool, and even the boss smiled. I thought, 'Is this because of the beans and brown bread?' Maybe, hey. I felt proud, and I started to think: if these foods make work easier, maybe they can make life a bit sweeter too, without needing all that sugar. Now, I look for more ways to eat smart and show others that us kasi boys can stay strong the healthy way.

input.story:
One morning, I tried to quickly pack little snack boxes for the crèche before heading to a dance practice. I made homemade pap with cheap cabbage and onions, but before we finished, I felt dizzy. Did I skip my insulin? Was it the heat, or did I not eat enough? I thought I knew how to look after myself, but I keep thinking, how does eating right matter when you’re moving non-stop? Hearing a child ask for a sandwich, I almost laughed—how am I supposed to afford bread for myself, let alone extras? When I sat down to rest, the small task wasn’t finished. The kids went without snacks, and I felt like I’d failed them.

Later that week, Sister Dudu, our local clinic [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE], noticed I wasn’t myself at the taxi rank. She greeted me, ‘Participant, you’re so quiet today, is everything all right?’ I shrugged. ‘Eating healthy is too expensive, [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]. And I’m tired!’ She listened and told me that even with little money, I could make healthy choices at home—like mabele porridge instead of pap, using tinned beans and fresh tomatoes, lots of water, and adding amadumbe or sweet potatoes if I can find them. She said, ‘It’s not about fancy food, just balancing what you have. And you can still cook your traditional dishes, just use less oil and salt. Small changes, Participant.’ Eish, could it be that simple?

The next days, I tried her ideas. I boiled amadumbe with spices and made a big pot of vegetable stew. But let me tell you, my body wanted bread and fried things, the way I used to make. I got tired and nearly gave up. Still, there was a big crèche event coming—a cultural dancing day for the kids—and I wanted to be strong for my dancing, and to prepare enough for everyone. Every time I felt like eating amagwinya, I remembered the [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]’s words. I slipped once, buying a vetkoek from Auntie Zanele, but I reminded myself, change is hard. Ek se, won’t life reward me if I just keep going?

Slowly, things began to get easier. I started feeling lighter. My energy lasted through umxhentso practice and I finished all the snacks for the big event, this time with bean stew, carrot sticks, and slices of fruit I got from the hawker. Seeing the kids smile and sharing my food with them made my heart happy. I even taught them a dance! Now, I’m thinking—maybe I really can keep eating better and feeling good, even with little money. Who would have thought a clinic [REDACTED_PROFILE_ATTRIBUTE]’s simple advice would help me so much?
